In 2005 I visited Russia for 20 days. First, at Aeroflot check in they didn't have me fill out any forms and didn't snoop in my luggage. They just looked at my visa and let me board. When I landed they didn't question me and didn't look at my luggage in Moscow either. Taking the train to Shakhty was no bother either. Just a long 24 hour trip on a slow train but it was fun. You can walk to the caboose where they feed you or just bring your own food. Only issue I had was I didn't understand what type of room to get on the train so I was stuck with two gorgeous Russian gals and my girlfriend who was pissed off. Personally, I liked the Russian gals quite a bit. Anyway, in Shakhty I registered with local police as required but they were just a bunch of grumpy bored guys at the creepy police station. Warning signs on all their office rooms to not enter unless authorized and instead of locking doors they have a string in a wax seal. It was like they were living in medieval age.

What I'm saying is that no one bothered me at all for anything. The people were great and extremely welcoming and hospitable. They love the novelty of having Americans visit. The Russian language was easy to pick up so language didn't seem to be much of a problem for me. I've forgotten most of the words I learned but I hope to go back. Once you learn the alphabet you'll notice many important words are basically borrowed words from English. Most important phrase I guess would be "Ya Hachoo Toilet" Next would be "Ya Hachoo kusich". Which means, I want to eat. After that phrases just start becoming easier.

My Russian girlfriend took me the second day to a market which is somewhat like a swap meet with sellers manning booths where they sell the particular food they produce. Hilariously my girlfriend was pointing at various vegetables and saying what I thought was "potato". I was confused. Everything was "Potato". That can't be right I thought. What she was saying was, "Vo Te Eto?". "You want this?" We got lots of "potatoes" of all kinds cause I just said "Da" every time. Just a large bag of various vegetables.

If you have business skills and want to start a business obviously you should make a visit in the area you wish to be and just walk around looking at businesses and ask questions once you are settled in. Do try to find someone you can trust as a guide. I suggest Southern Russia just because I don't like the extreme weather of Moscow. An American themed restaurant would be a great idea but there's all sorts of opportunities in Russia for a savvy American. One thing Rostov didn't have was decent Pizza. I got personal Pizza for my girlfriend, her son and myself. Mine came with sauce I asked for but it turned out to be crappy Russian ketchup. My girlfriend and her son got regular "pizza" which was just the dough with bits of cheese and not that much cheese anyway. Shakhty did have one fairly decent restaurant that served expensive food but the service was great. The waitress stood by our table like a slave, refilling my water, changing out napkins and basically pampering us. Best thing of all was the theater run by the local university because the director heard I would be attending and made the ending a bit of a dig poking fun of America. Ok, I can take a joke!

Here's the real shock I got on my return to USA. Coming in I was pulled aside and interrogated like I was a criminal. They searched every item in my luggage and bitched like hell about a bit of cheese I brought with me and forgot to put on my list of declared items. I had a small jar of honey they wanted to take away from me and at that point I finally lost my temper saying, "What, a jar of honey is a national security problem? Seriously guys?". They laughed and told me to pack up and go catch my plane to the final destination.

This is what I puzzled over on the final leg of my trip. Why, going to Russia they just didn't give a rats ass and the hundred pounds of food, chocolate and other stuff. They didn't even look. I wasn't searched, I wasn't questioned and the one time police in Moscow questioned me I just showed my passport and they walked away like nothing had happened. I have no idea what the Moscow police asked me but it was very polite so I just took out my passport and like magic they were gone. I was told later that they were concerned by my beard and thought I might be Chechen. So why the difference between USA and Russia on security?

One solid reason for police not being interested is that as a foreigner you are off limits to local police departments.

Another idea I have on why they don't bother you coming in is because maybe they figure you'd be insane to start shit in Russia. Seriously, they may not have a gulag but you don't want to be in a Russian jail for any reason. Russians don't seem to be the overly suspicious or paranoid types.

As for the people you might notice something right away. In public Russians don't smile. They look either bored or grim. The reason for this is that Russians have a cultural thing where in their mind a person who smiles for no obvious reason is either a moronic idiot or a criminal. If a Russian guy comes up to you smiling, be cautious. An expression I heard is to "Beware mousetraps". Meaning, don't go places with strangers. That's a set up to "mousetrap" you. Russians are very fond of ironic jokes and polite sarcasm when offended. They love playing elaborate jokes on people they like. I was pranked at a dinner with cold fermented potato soup which made everyone laugh their asses off. They must have planned it days in advance I guess because I was told that it wasn't usually served in winter time but was a summertime treat. They knew it would surprise me as we don't have such a thing in USA. My favorite thing to drink in Russia was Kvass which is made from spiced fermented bread and water. Imagine my surprise when I found it at a small Russian shop in Sacramento. It's a bit like Root Beer so it tastes very familiar.
